title: Nickel and Dimed: On (Not) Getting By in America
author: Barbara Ehrenreich
target_audience: General readers interested in social and economic issues
Students and scholars of sociology, economics, and labor studies
Individuals concerned with poverty, labor rights, and minimum wage policies
core_themes: Poverty and the working poor in America
Dignity and exploitation in the workplace
primary_purpose: To investigate and expose the harsh realities faced by low-wage workers in America by documenting the author's firsthand experiences working in various minimum-wage jobs, challenging myths about poverty and self-sufficiency.

structure_format.narrative_style: First-person investigative reporting blended with personal reflection, social analysis, and journalistic storytelling
structure_format.organization: Chronological narrative divided by the author’s experiences in different cities and jobs (waitress, hotel maid, cleaning woman, Walmart associate)
features: Reflections on personal privilege and limitations of the experiment

key_concepts_lessons: Even with multiple low-wage jobs, it is extremely difficult to afford basic housing, food, and healthcare in America.
The work performed by low-wage employees is physically and mentally demanding, often stigmatized, and undervalued.
Structural challenges—such as lack of affordable housing, transportation, and healthcare—keep workers trapped in cycles of poverty.
The myth that anyone willing to work hard can succeed in America does not reflect the reality for many low-income workers.
Systematic exploitation and dehumanization are prevalent in low-wage labor sectors.
Experiencing poverty is not solely a matter of bad choices but is deeply rooted in economic and social policies.
notable_features: Combines personal experience with socio-economic analysis
Highlights invisible struggles of America’s working poor
Influential in public debates on minimum wages and labor policy
cultural_historical_context: Published at the start of the 21st century, during a period of economic expansion in the U.S. but growing concern about widening inequality and stagnant minimum wages. The book draws on the aftermath of welfare reform in the 1990s, offering a counter-narrative to dominant ideals of American upward mobility.
reception_impact: Bestseller and widely discussed upon release
Praised for shedding light on the lived experience of low-wage workers
Influenced discussions around minimum wage, labor rights, and poverty policy
Criticized by some for the author’s temporary immersion versus lived lifetime experience of poverty
Frequently cited in academic, journalistic, and policy debates
